title: What a website is
plain: A website is a set of pages and files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images) that a server sends to your browser when you ask for them.
check: What has to happen before a friend in another country can see the index.html that you saved on your laptop?
rubric: Says the file must be on a computer that is online and runs a web server (hosting), not only on the laptop.
Says the friend needs a URL, a web address that points to that server.
Says the friend's browser sends a request, and the server sends back the HTML (and often CSS, JavaScript and images) for the browser to show.
try:
In a new scratch folder create index.html with this content: My first page

Hello, web

Open the file in your browser (double-click it, or drag it into a browser window). You see 'Hello, web' as a large heading, and the tab is called 'My first page'. In most browsers the address bar starts with file://, which means the page comes from your own disk, not from a server.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a page that opens in my browser is already online. Correct: an address that starts with file:// is a file on your own disk that only you can see; other people need a server to serve the files.

title: HTML
plain:
HTML is the text format that describes what is on a web page. Tags such as

and

mark each part as a heading, a paragraph, a link or an image.
check: In Docs, which part does a visitor read on the page, and which part tells the browser where to go?
rubric: Names Docs, the text between the opening and closing tags, as the part a visitor reads.
Names the href attribute, which holds the web address, as the part that tells the browser where to go.
Says and are the opening and closing tag of the link element, and that the page shows the change after a reload.
try:
Open the index.html you made earlier (or any .html file) in your editor. Inside , after the

line, add:

About

I am learning from MDN Web Docs.

Save the file and reload the browser tab (F5). You see a smaller heading, a paragraph and a link you can click.
pitfall: Wrong belief: HTML is a programming language that makes things happen. Correct: HTML only describes content and structure; behavior, such as reacting to a click, comes from JavaScript.

title: CSS
plain: CSS is a set of rules that controls how HTML elements look: color, size, spacing and layout. A rule has a selector and properties, like h1 { color: red; }.
check: In the rule p { color: blue; }, which part picks WHAT to style and which part says HOW to style it?
rubric: Names p as the selector, which picks what to style.
Names color: blue, a property and its value inside the braces, as how to style it.
Says one rule can hold several properties, each ending with a semicolon, and that index.html needs a link element to load style.css.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if my CSS change shows nothing, CSS is broken. Correct: the browser may show an old cached file, the selector may not match, or another rule may win; the Styles pane in the developer tools shows which rules apply.

title: Browser developer tools
plain: Developer tools are a panel built into your browser. It shows the page's HTML and CSS, error messages in the Console, and every request in the Network tab.
check: A page looks broken. Which tab do you open to see a red JavaScript error, and which tab do you open to see whether a file failed to download?
rubric: Opens the tools with F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I (Cmd+Option+I on a Mac)
Names the Elements, Console and Network tabs and what each shows
Finds the row for the main page in the Network tab and reads its Status
try: Open https://example.com in your browser. Press F12 (on a Mac laptop: Cmd+Option+I). Click the Network tab, then reload the page (F5). Click the first row, named example.com: its Status is 200 and its Type is document (Firefox shows html). Now click the Console tab: it is usually empty. You changed nothing on the website.
pitfall: Wrong belief: editing a page in the developer tools changes the real website. Correct: the edit changes only the copy in your browser and disappears when you reload; it never reaches the server.

title: URL
plain: A URL is a web address. It has a scheme (https), a host (example.com), an optional port, a path (/docs), an optional query (?page=2) and an optional fragment (#top).
check: What is different between https://shop.example/items and https://shop.example/items?color=red, and who uses the part after the question mark?
rubric: Says the second address has a query, ?color=red, that sends extra data to the server: here a filter for the color red.
Says the server's program reads the query, while the path /items stays the same.
Says the fragment (#...) is different: the browser keeps it and does not send it to the server.
try:
Run this line (python3 on macOS and Linux):
python -c "from urllib.parse import urlparse; u = urlparse('https://example.com:8080/docs/intro?lang=en#top'); print(u.scheme, u.hostname, u.port, u.path, u.query, u.fragment)"
It prints: https example.com 8080 /docs/intro lang=en top. Each word is one part of the URL. Nothing is sent over the internet.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the path in a URL is always a folder on the server. Correct: the path is text that the server's program interprets; it can name a file, but it can also start a function or a database lookup, like /users/42.

title: Requests and responses
plain: HTTP is how a client, such as a browser, talks to a server. The client sends a request (method and URL); the server answers with a response (status code and content).
check: You click a link that goes to /about. What does the browser send, what does it get back, and what does it do with it?
rubric: Says the browser sends a GET request for /about to the server.
Says the server sends back a response with a status code (200 for success) and content, usually HTML.
Says the browser reads the HTML, shows the page and may send more requests for CSS, JavaScript and images.
try: In the folder that holds your index.html run: python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 (python3 on macOS and Linux). Open http://localhost:8000 in the browser and reload once. The terminal prints lines like: 127.0.0.1 - - [07/Oct/2026 10:15:02] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -. Each line is one request from your browser: GET is the method, / is the path, 200 is the status. You may also see a /favicon.ico line with 404: the browser asks for a tab icon by itself. Press Ctrl+C to stop the server.
pitfall: Wrong belief: client and server are two different kinds of computer. Correct: they are roles in one conversation; when you run a local server and open it in your browser, your laptop plays both.

title: Status codes (200, 404, 500)
plain: A status code is a three-digit number in every HTTP response. 2xx means success, 3xx means go somewhere else, 4xx means a problem with the request, and 5xx means the server failed.
check: Your app returns 500 when you submit a form. Whose code most likely has the problem, the browser's or the server's, and where do you look first?
rubric: Says 5xx means the server failed, so the cause is in the server's code and not in the visitor's browser.
Says to look first at the server's error output or logs, where the error from that request is written.
Says a 4xx code would point at the request instead: a wrong address (404), a missing login (401) or no permission (403).
try: Start the local server again: python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 (python3 on macOS and Linux). Open http://localhost:8000/missing.html. The browser shows an error page with 'Error code: 404'. Open the developer tools (F12), click Network and reload: the row for missing.html shows Status 404, and the terminal prints 'code 404, message File not found'. Now open http://localhost:8000/ : the Status is 200. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a 404 or 500 means my computer or the internet is broken. Correct: an answer arrived, so the connection worked; 4xx points at the request (wrong address, no permission) and 5xx at a failure inside the server.

title: localhost and ports
plain: localhost means this same computer (address 127.0.0.1). A port is a number after the colon, like :3000, that tells your computer which running program should answer the request.
check: http://localhost:3000 shows your app on your laptop. A friend types the same address on their own computer. What do they see, and why?
rubric: Says the friend sees an error such as connection refused, or only their own computer's page, because localhost always means the computer they are typing on.
Says the app runs on your laptop, and nothing listens on port 3000 on their computer.
Names a way to show the app to others: put it on a host with a public address.
try:
Run this one line (python3 on macOS and Linux):
python -c "import socket; a=socket.socket(); a.bind(('127.0.0.1', 8123)); a.listen(); b=socket.socket(); b.bind(('127.0.0.1', 8123))"
It ends with an OSError. Windows: '[WinError 10048] Only one usage of each socket address ... is normally permitted'. macOS: '[Errno 48] Address already in use'. Linux: '[Errno 98] Address already in use'. The first socket took port 8123, the second asked for the same port and was refused. Nothing keeps running afterwards.
pitfall: Wrong belief: localhost is a website that everyone can open. Correct: localhost always means the computer you are typing on, so your friend's localhost is their own machine.

title: JavaScript in the browser
plain: In a web page, JavaScript is a programming language that runs inside your browser. It can react to clicks and change the page after it has loaded, without asking the server again.
check: Your script changes a paragraph when you click a button, but after you reload the page the old text is back. Why, and where would you have to change something to keep the new text?
rubric: Says the click handler changed the page in the browser's memory only, and the HTML file did not change.
Says a reload loads the original HTML again, so the change is lost.
Names where to keep the new text: the HTML file for fixed content, localStorage for this browser only, or a server with a database for everyone.
pitfall: Wrong belief: code in a web page is hidden from visitors. Correct: it runs on the visitor's computer, so anyone can read it with View Source or the developer tools; never put passwords or API keys in it.

title: APIs and endpoints
plain: An API is a way for one program to ask another program for data or actions. A web API receives HTTP requests at addresses called endpoints (like /users/42) and usually replies with JSON.
check: https://api.example.com/v1/users/42 returns JSON for one user. What do you expect for /v1/users/9999999 when no such user exists, and how would your program notice?
rubric: Sends a GET request to an endpoint and gets status 200
Reads two named fields from the JSON answer
Triggers a 404 on purpose and says what it means
try:
Needs internet (python3 on macOS and Linux). Run:
python -c "import json, urllib.request as u; r = u.urlopen('https://api.github.com/repos/python/cpython'); d = json.load(r); print(r.status, d['full_name'], d['language'])"
It prints: 200 python/cpython Python. That was a GET request to one endpoint, and you read two fields of the JSON answer. Now change cpython to cpythonx and run it again: it ends with 'HTTP Error 404: Not Found'. In the REST style the address names a thing and the method says the action: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH changes, DELETE removes. GitHub limits requests without a login per hour for each IP address, so do not run this in a loop.
pitfall: Wrong belief: an API is a product or a page you open. Correct: it is the set of rules for programs to talk to a service; a web API often has an address like a website's but returns data (JSON) instead of a page.

title: Cookies and sessions
plain: A cookie is a text value that your browser stores for a site and sends back with matching requests. A session is the server's record of you, usually found by an ID in a cookie.
check: You copy the value of your login cookie and send it to a friend, who pastes it into their own browser. What can they now do, and why is that dangerous?
rubric: Says the server finds the session by the ID in the cookie, so the friend's browser is treated as you until the session ends.
Says no password or second factor is asked for again, so a copied login cookie is as dangerous as a password.
Says never to share or paste cookie values, and that on most sites signing out or changing the password ends the old session.
try: Open a website where you are already signed in. Press F12, then open the Application tab (Chrome, Edge) or the Storage tab (Firefox), then Cookies, then click the site address. Only look: read the Name, Domain, Expires / Max-Age, HttpOnly and Secure columns. Do not edit, delete or copy any value. You see a table with several rows; the login cookie is often marked HttpOnly.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a cookie is a program that can run code or spy on me. Correct: a cookie is only text; what matters is who can read it, because a login cookie lets whoever holds it act as you, so it must stay secret and travel only over HTTPS.

title: Hosting, domains and DNS
plain: Hosting is using a computer, usually rented, that stays online and serves your files. A domain name (example.com) is a name you register. DNS turns that name into the server's IP address.
check: You just registered a domain name for your recipe site. What still has to exist, and what still has to be set, before a visitor sees your site at that name?
rubric: Checks that the host serves the site at its own address first
Checks that DNS points the domain to the host
Knows that a DNS change can take time to reach everyone
try:
Needs internet (python3 on macOS and Linux). Run:
python -c "import socket; print(socket.gethostbyname('example.com'))"
It prints an IP address: four numbers separated by dots (yours may differ from someone else's). That is the answer DNS gave your computer for the name example.com. Nothing is changed.
pitfall: Wrong belief: buying a domain name creates a website. Correct: the domain is only a name; you also need hosting that serves your files and DNS settings that point the name to that host.
